about: A file named, proved, and sometimes carried. The format could describe an attachment and never move one, which two unrelated clients hit independently — a canvas wanting a picture on a block, and a tablet wanting a lassoed region on one. These cases are what carrying it means, and what a consumer owes somebody when it is handed a name it cannot resolve.

cases.why: The shape v0 has always written. Everything else in this suite is additive on top of it, and the day a name alone stops validating is the day every export written before this suite becomes non-conformant — which is not a version bump anybody agreed to.

Bytes nobody can check are bytes nobody should trust. The hash is also how a consumer recognizes a second copy of a file it already holds, so bytes without one cannot be deduplicated and cannot be verified — the two things carrying them was for.

Sixty-four lowercase hex characters, so two producers computing the same hash write the same string. A format that accepts both cases of the same digest has an identity that compares unequal to itself.

The same rule as an empty string anywhere else in this format: omit rather than store nothing. An empty `bytes` reads as a file of length zero to a machine and as an absent file to a person, and the one real empty file in a library is not worth that ambiguity in every other.

The heart of it. A hash with no bytes is a *known-missing* file: the consumer knows a file exists, knows exactly which one, and does not have it. Importing that as though the attachment were absent is the silent coercion this format exists to prevent — the library looks complete and is not, and nobody finds out until they open the note.

The other half of the pair, and the reason the first is not simply a warning about attachments in general. A consumer that got the file reports nothing, so a `reduced` on this suite always means a specific file is missing rather than that attachments were involved.

A hash nobody checks is a comment. This is the one case in the suite where the producer is wrong rather than merely unable, and a consumer that stored the bytes anyway would be spreading a file it has been told is not the file it was promised.

This case is why `format` does not bump. A consumer written before any of this existed treats `sha256` and `bytes` as unknown keys, and the round-trip rule already obliges it to hand them back untouched. The addition is safe because that rule was there first — not because every consumer will be updated.

`attachments` says attachment values travel; `attachment-bytes` says the files do. One word covering both is a promise the data does not keep — a consumer reading `attachments` and planning storage for what arrives has no way to know whether anything will. Declaring the second is how it finds out before it starts rather than per file.
